identity.title: Differential Drive Kinematics
identity.tagline: The math behind nearly every simple wheeled robot: how two independent wheel speeds combine into forward motion and turning.

simpleSummary: The math for how two independently-driven wheels' speeds combine to move a robot forward, backward, or turn it — spin the wheels at the same speed and it drives straight, spin them at different speeds and it turns.
keyIdea: A differential-drive robot's forward speed is the average of its two wheel speeds, and its turning rate is proportional to the difference between them — which is exactly why most simple wheeled robots use two independently-driven wheels rather than a steering mechanism.
overview: A differential-drive robot has two wheels mounted on a common axis, each driven by its own independent motor, plus (usually) a passive caster wheel for balance. 'Differential' refers to the difference between the two wheels' speeds, not any physical difference between the wheels themselves. This simple two-motor arrangement, with no separate steering mechanism at all, is capable of driving straight, turning gradually, or even rotating in place — all purely by choosing the two wheel speeds correctly — which is exactly why it's the default drivetrain for the overwhelming majority of hobby wheeled robots, from simple line-followers to robot vacuums.

equations.label: Robot Linear Velocity
equations.meaning: The robot's forward speed v is the average of the two wheels' surface speeds, where r is wheel radius and ω_R, ω_L are the right and left wheel's angular velocities.

equations.label: Robot Angular Velocity
equations.meaning: The robot's turning rate ω is proportional to the difference between the two wheel speeds, divided by L, the track width (the distance between the two wheels).

howItWorks: Each wheel's own surface speed is simply its radius times its angular velocity (v_wheel = r·ω_wheel). The robot's overall forward velocity is the average of the two wheels' surface speeds — if both wheels spin identically, the average equals each wheel's speed and the robot drives in a perfectly straight line, since there's no speed difference to cause turning. The robot's turning rate depends entirely on the difference between the two wheel speeds: the larger the difference (relative to how far apart the wheels are), the sharper the turn. A special and very useful case is ω_R = −ω_L (the two wheels spinning at equal speed but opposite directions): the linear velocity term (their average) becomes exactly zero while the angular velocity term (their difference) is at its maximum — the robot rotates precisely in place around the midpoint between its wheels, with zero net forward motion. In practice, robot code works in the opposite direction from these equations: given a desired forward speed and a desired turn rate (often from a joystick, a line-following sensor error, or a path-planning algorithm), the code inverts these two equations to compute the individual left and right wheel speeds (and therefore PWM values) needed to actually produce that combined motion.
diagramCaption: Different wheel speeds curve the robot's path around an instantaneous center of curvature; equal wheel speeds drive straight, and equal-and-opposite speeds rotate the robot in place around its own midpoint.
realWorldExamples: This site's Line-Following Robot and Obstacle-Avoidance Robot projects both use exactly this two-motor differential-drive scheme through an L298N motor driver.
Robot vacuum cleaners (like classic Roomba-style robots) use differential drive, spinning their two wheels independently to navigate and turn in place.
Electric wheelchairs commonly use differential drive, with independently controlled left and right wheel motors giving full maneuverability without any separate steering linkage.
commonMisconceptions: "Each wheel just needs to spin at the target robot speed" — both wheels' individual speeds must be computed together from both the desired forward speed and the desired turn rate; setting them independently doesn't produce controllable motion.

"Differential drive means the two wheels are physically different from each other" — 'differential' refers to the difference in their speeds (which produces turning), not any physical difference between the wheels themselves.

"Differential drive robots can move sideways" — they cannot; like any standard wheeled robot, they can only drive along the direction the wheels point and turn by curving that direction, unlike a mecanum-wheeled robot.
